query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy, elevated-temperature degradation is governed by the selective oxidation of Ti and Cr that forms a dual-layer, self-healing oxide scale under oxidizing conditions. Under reducing atmospheres, the absence of such a protective scale accelerates grain-boundary diffusion and elemental segregation, which eventually compromises the microstructural integrity even though the FCC matrix initially retains its strength and fatigue performance.
generation.material_initial_state: An additively manufactured alloy with a uniform, nanocrystalline FCC matrix designed for high strength and fatigue resistance.
generation.intervention: Exposure to elevated temperatures (e.g., 700–900 °C) in controlled oxidizing (e.g., air) versus reducing (e.g., H2-rich) gas environments.
generation.conditions: Extended exposure (e.g., hundreds of hours) at high temperatures where kinetic diffusion processes are active; one set of samples exposed to oxidizing conditions and a parallel set to reducing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation (or lack) of a continuous, nanocrystalline oxide scale—primarily comprised of Ti-rich and Cr-rich oxides—at the surface and along grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Under oxidizing conditions, the preferential oxidation of Ti and Cr leads to the in situ development of an adherent dual-layer oxide scale that acts as a diffusion barrier, thereby preserving the underlying FCC matrix. In contrast, reducing environments do not facilitate this protective oxide formation, resulting in accelerated elemental migration along grain boundaries that ultimately weakens the microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples exposed to oxidizing gases will develop a thin, continuous oxide scale with minimal loss in mechanical properties, while those exposed to reducing gases will show signs of grain-boundary segregation, microcracking, and degraded mechanical performance over similar timescales.
generation.baseline: The as-built nanocrystalline FCC matrix exhibiting high strength and fatigue performance without significant oxidation or elemental segregation.
generation.boundary: Temperature range of approximately 700–900 °C and exposure durations long enough (e.g., 100–1000 hours) for the kinetics of oxidation and diffusion processes to become significant.
generation.uncertainty: The precise composition, structure, and protective efficacy of the oxide scale under varying oxidizing conditions remain to be fully determined, as do the quantitative rates of diffusion and segregation under reducing environments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare sets of identical Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 samples and expose one set to an oxidizing environment (air at 800 °C) and another set to a reducing environment (e.g., H2-rich atmosphere at 800 °C) for 500 hours. Characterize the surface and grain-boundary regions using TEM, XPS, and XRD, and assess mechanical properties via nanoindentation and fatigue testing before and after exposure.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness, continuity, and composition (using TEM, XPS, and XRD)
Changes in mechanical properties (nanoindentation hardness, tensile strength, fatigue life)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both oxidizing and reducing conditions yield similar oxide scale characteristics and comparable degradation in mechanical performance, or if the oxidizing environment fails to form a continuous protective oxide layer relative to the reducing case, then the hypothesis is falsified.

System: CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy (equimolar or nearly equimolar proportions of Cobalt, Chromium, Iron, Nickel, and Titanium).
